items.title: nokia-applied-research/AnyJev
items.excerpt: Turn any LLM into a Jev-style decision model: typed decisions, real probabilities, no training. (continue updating, welcome any issue and PR request)
items.summary: Nokia AnyJev authors report converting any LLM into typed decision models with real probabilities, requiring no training.
items.usefulness: Could help Python developers structure LLM outputs as constrained decision types if the probability calibration claim holds.
items.to_verify: Whether 'real probabilities' are calibrated and whether the approach works across diverse base models.

items.title: Show HN: Parsimony – an open-source benchmark for how much code AI models add
items.excerpt: Existing benchmarks measure solve rate and token output/cost, but don't punish excess code, which makes a codebase harder to work with in the long term. I wanted to measure this since it matters most for long-term projects. Method: it takes the patches that benchmarks already publish (DeepSWE, SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Live) and counts "coding units": syntax elements like statements, calls, names and literals. I didn't use lines of code, so cramming code isn't rewarded. Deleted code is subtracted, so it measures net units. GPT-6 and Claude 5.5 have no public patches yet, so I ran them myse
items.summary: Parsimony benchmark counts code units (statements, calls, names, literals) across model patches to penalize excess code addition, excluding lines-of-code metrics.
items.usefulness: Might help evaluate if Python AI coding tools produce maintainable patches, not just solve problems.
items.to_verify: Whether net unit counting actually correlates with long-term codebase health and maintainability.
